Double Sequences and Iterated Limits

This scene is about double sequences. Watch the values am,na_{m,n}am,n​ on a grid, and see how the row-wise and column-wise limits split apart.

The double limit lets both indices grow together. An iterated limit sends one index first, then the other. Swapping the order can change the answer. And even when both iterated limits agree, the double limit may not exist.

For example, reading a 📋 table row by row is not the same as reading it column by column. Change the reading order, and you can land on a completely different conclusion.

Prove the following theorem completely.

If a double sequence am,na_{m,n}am,n​ converges to LLL in the Pringsheim sense (for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 there is NNN with ∣am,n−L∣<ε|a_{m,n} - L| < \varepsilon∣am,n​−L∣<ε whenever m,n>Nm, n > Nm,n>N), and for each fixed mmm the inner limit bm=lim⁡n→∞am,nb_m = \lim_{n\to\infty} a_{m,n}bm​=limn→∞​am,n​ exists, then lim⁡m→∞bm=L\lim_{m\to\infty} b_m = Llimm→∞​bm​=L.

Conclude: when the double limit exists and both iterated limits exist, both iterated limits equal the double limit.

    Since ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 was arbitrary, lim⁡m→∞bm=L\lim_{m\to\infty} b_m = Llimm→∞​bm​=L: that is, lim⁡m→∞lim⁡n→∞am,n=L\lim_{m\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty} a_{m,n} = Llimm→∞​limn→∞​am,n​=L.

    Choosing an even n>N0n > N_0n>N0​ gives ∣1m−b∣<12m\left|\frac{1}{m} - b\right| < \frac{1}{2m}​m1​−b​<2m1​; choosing an odd n>N0n > N_0n>N0​ gives ∣−1m−b∣<12m\left|-\frac{1}{m} - b\right| < \frac{1}{2m}​−m1​−b​<2m1​.

    By the triangle inequality, 2m=∣(1m−b)+(b+1m)∣≤∣1m−b∣+∣−1m−b∣<12m+12m=1m\frac{2}{m} = \left|\left(\frac{1}{m} - b\right) + \left(b + \frac{1}{m}\right)\right| \le \left|\frac{1}{m} - b\right| + \left|-\frac{1}{m} - b\right| < \frac{1}{2m} + \frac{1}{2m} = \frac{1}{m}m2​=​(m1​−b)+(b+m1​)​≤​m1​−b​+​−m1​−b​<2m1​+2m1​=m1​ — the false inequality 2m<1m\frac{2}{m} < \frac{1}{m}m2​<m1​.

    This contradiction shows lim⁡n→∞am,n\lim_{n\to\infty} a_{m,n}limn→∞​am,n​ does not exist. Since this holds for every mmm, the iterated limit lim⁡m→∞lim⁡n→∞am,n\lim_{m\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty} a_{m,n}limm→∞​limn→∞​am,n​ does not exist.

    Hence lim⁡n→∞lim⁡m→∞am,n=lim⁡n→∞0=0\lim_{n\to\infty}\lim_{m\to\infty} a_{m,n} = \lim_{n\to\infty} 0 = 0limn→∞​limm→∞​am,n​=limn→∞​0=0, matching the double limit in (i).

    There is no conflict with the theorem of Problem 2: it only speaks about an order in which the inner limits exist, and here they exist in just one order.
